Test comment in test_tokenizer_reads_replace_as_a_keyword claims it pins the keyword token shape 'across the supported sqlglot range', but the test only runs against the installed sqlglot version, not the whole sqlglot>=25.0,<31 range.

CI comment cites MySQL errors 1418/1419, but the connector test's stored function declares READS SQL DATA, so 1418 does not apply; only 1419 (missing SUPER with binary logging on) is why the step exists.

The routine refusal message is always the generic 'functions defined in the database are not supported while row-level security is active' and never names the matched call; since matching is by name across every schema and keyword/type tokens before '(' are collected, a built-in call (e.g. max with citext installed) can be refused with a message that misleads the agent about which call to remove.

The child check refuses only relations that are themselves children; under PostgreSQL multiple inheritance (child INHERITS (orders, audit_base) with a rule only on orders), SELECT * FROM audit_base returns the child's rows unfiltered, and the Limitations bullet does not tell operators each parent of a multi-parent child needs its own rule.

## Verdict: APPROVE with notes (no finding or checklist FAIL at the critical threshold; one Important finding, six Suggestions and three inconclusive checklist items remain)
The PR is ready to merge: child tables, database-defined routine calls and the function blocklist under row-level security all fail closed, every acceptance criterion has a checklist item, and nothing remaining reaches the critical threshold.
Rule applied: rule 6 — findings and checklist FAILs below the threshold, and INCONCLUSIVE items, remain → APPROVE with notes

## Code Review Findings

### 🟠 Important / Major

1. `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` lines 248-252: the routine refusal always says "functions defined in the database are not supported while row-level security is active" and never names the matched call. Because matching is by name alone across every schema, and keyword or type tokens before `(` are also collected, a built-in call can be refused with this message when an extension installs a routine of the same name (for example citext's `max`), so the calling agent cannot tell which call to remove. The query is still blocked. (raised by 1/4 agents)

### 🟡 Suggestion / Minor (6)

<details><summary>6 items</summary>

1. `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` lines 178-186: `_verify_relations` raises a bare `TypeError` for a non-boolean child flag (and `row[3]` an `IndexError` for a short `pg_class` row); only the caller's broad handler in `verify_base_tables` turns these into a sanitized `RlsError`, so the fail-closed rule is not expressed by the function itself. (raised by 1/4 agents)
2. `tests/unit/test_rls_views.py` lines 592-593: the test comment says it pins the keyword token shape "across the supported sqlglot range", but the test only runs against the installed sqlglot version, not the whole `sqlglot>=25.0,<31` range. (raised by 1/4 agents) <!-- inertness: first-conjunct=held limb-one=held limb-two=held; evidence: test comment; making it true changes no test outcome; git grep of the phrase across the repository finds only the comment itself; not rendered outside the repository -->
3. `.github/workflows/ci.yml` lines 147-148: the comment cites MySQL errors 1418/1419, but the connector test's function declares `READS SQL DATA`, so only 1419 (missing SUPER while binary logging is on) applies. (raised by 1/4 agents) <!-- inertness: first-conjunct=held limb-one=held limb-two=held; evidence: YAML comment; the CI step runs the same either way; git grep of the phrase finds only the comment itself; workflow comment is not published -->
4. `src/sqllens/safety/relations.py` lines 165-189: the child check refuses only relations that are themselves children, so under PostgreSQL multiple inheritance (`CREATE TABLE c () INHERITS (orders, audit_base)` with a rule only on `orders`), `SELECT * FROM audit_base` returns `c`'s rows unfiltered; the Limitations bullet does not tell operators that each parent of a multi-parent child needs its own rule. (raised by 1/4 agents)
- VC-32: FAIL (suggestion) — The _called_names docstring asserts that sqlglot parses `strpos` to `StrPosition` and that keyword and type names before `(` (such as `IN (` and `DECIMAL(`) are collected and only cost a catalog match. [src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:87]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  First half holds: sqlglot parser.py:478 maps "STRPOS" to exp.StrPosition.from_arg_list. Second half is inaccurate. _called_names (relations.py:98-106) collects any token before L_PAREN whose text is in tokenizer KEYWORDS (e.g. IN, DECIMAL), and verify_base_tables (relations.py:124-132) passes them to _refuse_database_routines (relations.py:222-252), which raises RlsError if any non-system pg_proc / information_schema.ROUTINES function shares the name. So a keyword or type name before '(' costs more than a catalog match: if the database defines a routine named e.g. decimal, any statement using DECIMAL( is refused. The docstring's 'only cost a catalog match' omits this possible refusal (fail-closed, rare, but the stated cost is wrong).

  </details>

- VC-38: FAIL (suggestion) — The _called_names docstring asserts each name is returned as written, lower-cased and ASCII-lower-cased because PostgreSQL folds only ASCII in unquoted names. [src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:91]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  relations.py:91-92 docstring says PostgreSQL 'folds only ASCII in unquoted names'. PostgreSQL's downcase_identifier (scansup.c) also lower-cases high-bit bytes via tolower() when the database encoding is single-byte (e.g. LATIN1: unquoted Äfn folds to äfn). So the absolute statement is wrong for single-byte server encodings. Code at 104-106 returns as-written, str.lower() and ASCII-lower spellings, and the predicate at 236 also matches lower(proname), so the guard likely still covers such cases in practice, but the docstring rationale is inaccurate (true only for multibyte encodings such as UTF-8). Comment-only defect.

  </details>

</details>

### ℹ️ Informational — Deferred (3)

<details><summary>3 items</summary>

- VC-29: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — _called_names relies on sqlglot.Dialect.get_or_raise(dialect) returning a Dialect instance with a tokenize(sql) method, and on type(instance).tokenizer_class.KEYWORDS being a mapping keyed by upper-case keyword text, across the supported sqlglot>=25.0,<31 range. [src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:94]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  pyproject.toml:44 pins sqlglot>=25.0,<31. relations.py:94-96 uses Dialect.get_or_raise, type(d).tokenizer_class.KEYWORDS and d.tokenize(sql). In installed sqlglot 30.26.0 (/Users/the01geek/repos/sqllens/.venv/.../sqlglot/dialects/dialect.py) get_or_raise is a classmethod returning Dialect (l.1047), tokenize(self, sql) exists (l.1286), tokenizer_class is set per dialect class by the metaclass (l.316, base l.903), and Tokenizer.KEYWORDS is a dict[str, TokenType] (tokens.py:56,229) whose keys the tokenizer upper-cases for its trie (tokens.py:117). So the claim holds for 30.x. I found no sqlglot 25.x-29.x install to read, so the lower part of the range is not verified here.

  </details>

- VC-31: INCONCLUSIVE (important) — The verify_base_tables docstring asserts that on PostgreSQL and MySQL a name in call position that matches, ignoring case, a routine defined in the database is refused, whether or not the statement references a relation. [src/sqllens/safety/relations.py:118]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  Traced src/sqllens/safety/relations.py. _called_names (84-107) pairs tokens and collects any VAR/IDENTIFIER/KEYWORD token followed by L_PAREN. sqlglot attaches comments to tokens, so `fn/**/()` still pairs. Backticked or quoted identifiers are IDENTIFIER tokens. Names are returned as written, Python lower() and ASCII-lower. verify_base_tables (122-145) runs the routine check whether or not relations exist, and any non-RlsError failure fails closed. PostgreSQL predicate (236) matches exact or lower(proname), which covers ASCII folding of unquoted names and exact quoted names. Settled so far: the claim holds for ASCII names on PostgreSQL and MySQL. It is unsettled for non-ASCII MySQL names. The query compares LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) with Python-derived strings (245). Python str.lower() and MySQL LOWER() can disagree. For example, 'ΑΣ'.lower() gives final-sigma 'ας', while MySQL would give 'ασ'. Whether the comparison still matches depends on the collation of ROUTINE_NAME and the connection (general_ci may treat the two as equal). I cannot run MySQL here, so I did not run that check. Separately, the MySQL query only matches ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION', so a stored procedure is not matched. A procedure cannot be invoked in a SELECT call position, so the docstring's 'routine' is loose but not clearly wrong. Missing evidence: a live MySQL run of the non-ASCII case-folding comparison.

  </details>

- VC-53: INCONCLUSIVE (suggestion) — The test comment asserts the RLS rewrite emits STRPOS on sqlglot 25.x and POSITION on 30.x for a PostgreSQL strpos call. [tests/unit/test_rls_views.py:619]

  <details><summary>Evidence</summary>

  Verified the 30.x half: installed sqlglot 30.26.0 (.venv/.../sqlglot-30.26.0.dist-info) sqlglot/generators/postgres.py:416 has exp.StrPosition: strposition_sql(self, e, func_name="POSITION"), so 30.x emits POSITION. pyproject.toml:44 allows sqlglot>=25.0,<31, so both ranges are in scope. The 25.x half (emits STRPOS) could not be checked: no sqlglot 25.x source is present in any searched venv or worktree (the ones found are all 30.x, where the postgres generator lives in sqlglot/generators/), and I did not run pip install sqlglot==25.x. The test assertion itself ({'position','strpos'} & params) tolerates either name.

  </details>

</details>

acceptance_criteria:
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured on PostgreSQL, a statement that references a relation recorded as a child in `pg_inherits` is refused with `RlsError` before it executes. This covers a declarative partition (`PARTITION OF`) and a traditional inheritance child (`INHERITS`), at any depth and in any position (top-level `FROM`, join, subquery, CTE body), whether or not a rule names the child or its parent. A rule naming a child table no longer makes that child queryable. A query on the hierarchy's top-level table still runs and returns only rows that match that table's rules, including rows stored in its children.
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured on PostgreSQL or MySQL, and with `database.read_only` true or false, a statement is refused with `RlsError` before it executes when it uses call syntax (`name(...)`, schema-qualified or not) with a name that matches, ignoring case, the name of a routine defined in the database. On PostgreSQL that means any `pg_proc` entry outside the `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` schemas, extension-installed routines included. On MySQL it means any stored function listed in `information_schema.ROUTINES`. Matching uses the routine name alone, across every schema and every argument signature. It covers such calls in the select list, `FROM`, joins, filters, aggregates and window functions, including statements that reference no relation. The names checked are the names called in the SQL that will execute after the RLS rewrite, including calls sqlglot parses as recognized built-in function nodes.
- [ ] While RLS rules are active, the read-only guard's function blocklist applies even when `database.read_only` is false: a statement that calls a function on that blocklist is refused before it executes with `UnsafeSqlError`, which reaches the MCP client as the read-only guard's refusals do today. Only the blocklist check is added on that path; with `database.read_only` false, the statement-type checks (SELECT-only) do not start applying. With no RLS rules configured, behavior for either value of `database.read_only` is unchanged. Unit tests cover, with `database.read_only` false: a blocklisted call under a rule refused; a statement that the RLS rewrite accepts but the SELECT-only checks would refuse (for example a PostgreSQL data-modifying CTE on a table without a rule) not refused by the new check; and a blocklisted call with no rules configured not refused, as today.
- [ ] Functions on the read-only guard's function blocklist are blocked while rules are active, whatever `database.read_only` is: with `database.read_only` true by the existing read-only guard, and with it false by the previous criterion. This change leaves the blocklist's entries as they are; the blocklist additions are delivered in a separate change.
- [ ] With an RLS rule configured, the routine check and the blocklist check do not refuse a statement whose called names are all outside the read-only guard's function blocklist and match no routine name that the database-defined routine check looks up, and such a statement that the other RLS checks accept keeps running with its rule predicates applied. Tests cover at minimum `count(*)` and `upper()` on PostgreSQL and MySQL, plus a PostgreSQL call that sqlglot parses as a typed node with a different canonical name (`strpos`).
- [ ] When a child or routine catalog lookup raises any exception, or the child lookup returns a child flag that is not a boolean, the query is refused with an `RlsError` whose message carries no driver detail. The cause is logged with a traceback, as for the existing relation lookup. A SQL text the check's sqlglot step cannot parse or tokenize is also refused with `RlsError`. The refusal is the same exception type through the same wrappers as the existing view refusal, so it reaches the MCP client exactly as a view refusal does, never as rows.
- [ ] Apart from the blocklist criterion, SQLite RLS behavior is unchanged: SQLite runs no child or routine lookup, and its existing RLS tests pass unmodified.
- [ ] Unit tests in `tests/unit/test_rls_views.py` drive `verify_base_tables` and the PostgreSQL and MySQL runners with fake cursors. They cover at minimum: child refused; a parent that is not a child allowed; a function call with no relation reference refused; a matching name in another schema or another letter case refused; a call whose name the sqlglot tokenizer reads as a keyword (for example `replace`), with a matching routine, refused; a built-in-only call allowed; and a raising lookup and a non-boolean child flag, both refused without echoing the driver detail. A routine lookup that returns no row allows the call.
- [ ] Connector tests in `tests/connectors/test_connectors.py` against real PostgreSQL create two protected parents: a partitioned table with a `PARTITION OF` child, and an ordinary table with an `INHERITS` child. They assert that each child query is blocked and that each parent query returns only scoped rows. They also create a SQL function that reads the protected table, and assert that calling it is blocked unqualified and schema-qualified. Against real MySQL, they create a stored function that reads the protected table and assert that both the unqualified and the schema-qualified call are blocked. On both engines, a built-in-only query on the protected table still returns scoped rows.
- [ ] In `docs/external/row-level-security.md#limitations`, the bullet opening "Rules match table names, not every path to the same rows" is replaced, and no Limitations bullet tells operators to add a rule per child table. The new bullet states that partition and inheritance child tables are unavailable while RLS is active and that rules belong on the top-level table. A second statement says that on PostgreSQL, calls to functions outside the `pg_catalog` and `information_schema` schemas, extension functions included, and on MySQL, calls to stored functions, are blocked while RLS is active, and that a built-in call is also blocked when such a function shares its name. The bullet keeps a least-privilege instruction to grant the SQL Lens database user `EXECUTE` only on routines the operator has reviewed. It does not claim that SQL Lens inspects every way the database can run stored code.
- [ ] In `docs/internal/database-connectors/row-level-security.md`, the "Database relation checks" section describes the child check (`pg_inherits`) and the routine check (`pg_proc` outside `pg_catalog`/`information_schema`; MySQL `information_schema.ROUTINES`; case-insensitive name match; runs with no relation references), and their fail-closed lookups. The paragraph opening "Known gaps with the same root cause" no longer describes these two paths as open. "Unprotected base-table queries still work" names the child-table exception. The custom-runner paragraph states that runners beneath `RlsGuardRunner` must enforce these checks too. The sentences in `docs/internal/database-connectors/read-only-safety.md` and in this page that say `database.read_only = false` skips the parser guard state that the function blocklist still applies while RLS rules are configured.
- [ ] A `changelog.d/<PR>.security.md` fragment states the outcome and the operator action: query top-level tables and move child rules to the parent, and note that, under RLS, calls to PostgreSQL functions outside `pg_catalog`/`information_schema` and to MySQL stored functions are blocked, and that while rules are active the read-only guard's function blocklist applies even when `database.read_only` is false. `changelog.d/274.security.md` is unchanged.

checklist.evidence: pyproject.toml:44 pins sqlglot>=25.0,<31. relations.py:94-96 uses Dialect.get_or_raise, type(d).tokenizer_class.KEYWORDS and d.tokenize(sql). In installed sqlglot 30.26.0 (/Users/the01geek/repos/sqllens/.venv/.../sqlglot/dialects/dialect.py) get_or_raise is a classmethod returning Dialect (l.1047), tokenize(self, sql) exists (l.1286), tokenizer_class is set per dialect class by the metaclass (l.316, base l.903), and Tokenizer.KEYWORDS is a dict[str, TokenType] (tokens.py:56,229) whose keys the tokenizer upper-cases for its trie (tokens.py:117). checklist.claim: The verify_base_tables docstring asserts that on PostgreSQL and MySQL a name in call position that matches, ignoring case, a routine defined in the database is refused, whether or not the statement references a relation.
checklist.source_excerpt:
On PostgreSQL and MySQL a name in call
    position that matches, ignoring case, a routine defined in the database is
    refused, whether or not the statement references a relation.
checklist.verify_hint: Trace inputs that could falsify it: a call whose name token is neither VAR/IDENTIFIER nor in the tokenizer KEYWORDS; a comment between the name and `(` (e.g. `fn/**/()`); a MySQL routine with a non-ASCII name whose case folding by MySQL's LOWER() differs from Python's str.lower(); a statement that fails `_relations` before `_called_names` runs (refused anyway). Check `_called_names` pairwise token logic and the `LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) IN (...)` / `lower(p.proname::text) = ANY(...)` predicates.
checklist.evidence: Traced src/sqllens/safety/relations.py. _called_names (84-107) pairs tokens and collects any VAR/IDENTIFIER/KEYWORD token followed by L_PAREN. sqlglot attaches comments to tokens, so `fn/**/()` still pairs. Backticked or quoted identifiers are IDENTIFIER tokens. Names are returned as written, Python lower() and ASCII-lower. verify_base_tables (122-145) runs the routine check whether or not relations exist, and any non-RlsError failure fails closed. PostgreSQL predicate (236) matches exact or lower(proname), which covers ASCII folding of unquoted names and exact quoted names. Settled so far: the claim holds for ASCII names on PostgreSQL and MySQL. It is unsettled for non-ASCII MySQL names. The query compares LOWER(ROUTINE_NAME) with Python-derived strings (245). Python str.lower() and MySQL LOWER() can disagree. For example, 'ΑΣ'.lower() gives final-sigma 'ας', while MySQL would give 'ασ'. Whether the comparison still matches depends on the collation of ROUTINE_NAME and the connection (general_ci may treat the two as equal). I cannot run MySQL here, so I did not run that check. Separately, the MySQL query only matches ROUTINE_TYPE='FUNCTION', so a stored procedure is not matched. A procedure cannot be invoked in a SELECT call position, so the docstring's 'routine' is loose but not clearly wrong. Missing evidence: a live MySQL run of the non-ASCII case-folding comparison.

checklist.claim: The _called_names docstring asserts that sqlglot parses `strpos` to `StrPosition` and that keyword and type names before `(` (such as `IN (` and `DECIMAL(`) are collected and only cost a catalog match.

sqlglot renames many
    built-ins (``strpos`` parses to ``StrPosition``), and a keyword such as
    ``replace`` is a call name too. Keyword and type names before ``(``
    (``IN (``, ``DECIMAL(``) are collected as well; they only cost a catalog

checklist.verify_against: sqlglot postgres parser FUNCTIONS mapping and the _refuse_database_routines lookup
checklist.verify_hint: Check `Postgres.Parser.FUNCTIONS` in sqlglot/dialects/postgres.py for STRPOS -> exp.StrPosition; note that a collected keyword such as `in`, `as` or `decimal` also refuses the statement if a database routine of that name exists (trace `_refuse_database_routines`), so check whether 'only cost a catalog match' holds.
checklist.evidence: First half holds: sqlglot parser.py:478 maps "STRPOS" to exp.StrPosition.from_arg_list. Second half is inaccurate. _called_names (relations.py:98-106) collects any token before L_PAREN whose text is in tokenizer KEYWORDS (e.g. IN, DECIMAL), and verify_base_tables (relations.py:124-132) passes them to _refuse_database_routines (relations.py:222-252), which raises RlsError if any non-system pg_proc / information_schema.ROUTINES function shares the name. So a keyword or type name before '(' costs more than a catalog match: if the database defines a routine named e.g. decimal, any statement using DECIMAL( is refused. The docstring's 'only cost a catalog match' omits this possible refusal (fail-closed, rare, but the stated cost is wrong).

checklist.verify_against: PostgreSQL identifier folding (downcase_identifier in src/backend/parser/scansup.c, which also lower-cases high-bit bytes in single-byte encodings) and the pg_proc predicate in _refuse_database_routines
checklist.verify_hint: Trace an unquoted non-ASCII routine name (e.g. `SELECT Äfn()`) through `_called_names` and the `p.proname::text = ANY(%s) OR lower(p.proname::text) = ANY(%s)` predicate; check whether the as-written, `str.lower()` and ASCII-lower spellings cover every stored proname for that call under UTF-8 and single-byte server encodings.
checklist.evidence: relations.py:91-92 docstring says PostgreSQL 'folds only ASCII in unquoted names'. PostgreSQL's downcase_identifier (scansup.c) also lower-cases high-bit bytes via tolower() when the database encoding is single-byte (e.g. LATIN1: unquoted Äfn folds to äfn). So the absolute statement is wrong for single-byte server encodings. Code at 104-106 returns as-written, str.lower() and ASCII-lower spellings, and the predicate at 236 also matches lower(proname), so the guard likely still covers such cases in practice, but the docstring rationale is inaccurate (true only for multibyte encodings such as UTF-8). Comment-only defect.
